title: General Overview
subject: Lymphoid System
introMarkdown:
The lymphatic system recovers fluid that escapes from blood vessels, helps defend the body against infection, and transports much of the fat absorbed by the small intestine. Its vessels, nodes, and lymphoid organs form a network linking fluid balance with immune surveillance.

**Lymphatic vessels** move fluid from tissues back toward the bloodstream. **Lymphoid tissues and organs** support the immune cells that recognize threats and coordinate defenses. Together, these functions make the system both a transport network and an essential part of immunity.

sections.title: Three Jobs, One System
sections.markdown:
The system has **three core functions**:

- **Fluid recovery:** Returns excess tissue fluid and proteins to the blood, helping prevent **edema** (swelling).
- **Immune defense:** Carries material from tissues through lymph nodes, where immune cells can examine it and organize responses.
- **Fat transport:** Moves chylomicron-rich fluid from intestinal **lacteals** toward the bloodstream.

One network can therefore recover fluid from your ankle, monitor material entering through your skin, and transport dietary fat from the intestine.

sections.title: From Blood Plasma to Interstitial Fluid to Lymph
sections.markdown:
**Blood plasma** is the fluid portion of blood. When fluid filters into spaces between cells, it becomes **interstitial fluid**. Once it enters a lymphatic capillary, it is called **lymph**.

**Initial lymphatic capillaries** begin as blind-ended vessels. Overlapping endothelial cells form flap-like openings that admit excess fluid when pressure in the surrounding tissue rises.

**Route:** Blood plasma → interstitial fluid → lymphatic capillaries → collecting vessels → lymphatic trunks and ducts → veins.

sections.title: The One-Way Route Back to Blood
sections.markdown:
There is **no central lymphatic pump** like the heart. **One-way valves**, skeletal-muscle movement, breathing-related pressure changes, and rhythmic contractions in lymphatic vessels help lymph move toward the chest.

- **Thoracic duct:** Returns lymph from most of the body, including both lower limbs and the upper-left region.
- **Right lymphatic duct:** Typically drains the upper-right region.
- **Cisterna chyli:** Expanded collecting region near the beginning of the thoracic duct.

Both major terminal routes deliver lymph to venous blood near the **internal jugular–subclavian vein junctions**.

sections.title: Three Major Lymphocyte Classes
sections.markdown:
**Lymphocytes** are white blood cells central to immune recognition and defense. Three major classes are:

- **B cells:** Can develop into antibody-secreting **plasma cells** and contribute to immune memory.
- **T cells:** **Helper T cells** coordinate defenses; **cytotoxic T cells** can kill infected or abnormal cells; regulatory populations restrain responses.
- **Natural killer (NK) cells:** Rapidly respond to certain infected, stressed, or abnormal cells as part of **innate immunity**.

B cells develop mainly in **bone marrow**, while immature T cells complete important stages of development in the **thymus**.

sections.title: Where Immune Cells Develop and Meet
sections.markdown:
- **Lymph nodes:** Filter **lymph** arriving from tissues and provide meeting places for immune cells.
- **Thymus:** Supports T-cell development and selection.
- **Spleen:** Monitors **blood**, responds to blood-borne antigens, and removes aged or abnormal red blood cells.
- **Tonsils, Peyer's patches, and other MALT:** Help monitor material at mucosal surfaces, including the airways and digestive tract.

**Primary lymphoid organs** support lymphocyte development, especially bone marrow and thymus. **Secondary lymphoid organs and tissues** are major sites where mature immune cells encounter antigens.

sections.title: The Immediate Defenses
sections.markdown:
**Innate defenses** act quickly without requiring a previous encounter with a particular pathogen. They include:

- **Physical barriers:** Skin and protective mucous membranes.
- **Phagocytes:** Cells that engulf microbes and debris.
- **NK-cell surveillance:** Recognition of certain abnormal cells.
- **Interferons:** Signals that help neighboring cells resist viral infection.
- **Complement:** Proteins that mark targets, promote inflammation, or damage membranes.
- **Inflammation:** Local response that recruits defensive cells.
- **Fever:** Systemic temperature regulation during some immune responses.

**Redness, heat, swelling, and pain** are the four classic signs of inflammation.

sections.title: Specific Recognition and Immune Memory
sections.markdown:
**Adaptive immunity** targets particular antigens and relies heavily on **B and T lymphocytes**. **Antigen-presenting cells** display processed material to appropriate T cells, helping coordinate an effective response. Activated B cells may release **antibodies** that bind targets and support their removal.

After an initial infection or vaccination, some antigen-experienced cells persist as **memory cells**. A second encounter can therefore trigger a faster or stronger response. **Immune tolerance** helps prevent these powerful defenses from attacking the body's own healthy tissues.

sections.title: What You Should Be Able to Identify
sections.markdown:
For anatomical identification, know the **thoracic duct**, **right lymphatic duct**, **cisterna chyli**, major **lymph-node groups**, **thymus**, **spleen**, and **tonsils**.

For tissue identification, distinguish the **lymph-node cortex, paracortex, medulla, and hilum**; the **white and red pulp** of the spleen; and the **cortex and medulla** of the thymus.

The **Deep Dive** explains these structures and immune mechanisms in detail. **Exam Cram** provides rapid review of the essential terms, pathways, and comparisons.
